sections.COMMENTS:
ï»¿    **COMMENTS**
The geometry of this Source is based on geological and geomorphologic observations on the Lunigiana basin. The Source is a N-dipping pure normal fault. This source belongs to the northernmost segment of the Etrurian Fault System outcropping along the western margin of the Lunigiana basin.
The existence and position of this source follows the suggestion of several papers dealing with the Etrurian Fault System (EFS; Boncio et al., 2000).
According to Boncio et al. (2000), the EFS is a sytem of low-angle, NE-dipping normal faults, that runs from northern Tuscany to southern Umbria. The well-known Alto Tiberina Fault includes the central-southern termination of the EFS, and it is the best constrained part of this fault system.
The EFS is associated in Tuscany to the main extensional basins that dissect the northern Apennines, and in some cases host the seismogenic sources of large historical normal faulting earthquakes. From north to south they are: the Lunigiana, Garfagnana, Mugello and Casentino basins.
The Lunigiana and Garfagnana basins are two structural depressions limited by NW-SE extensional faults filled with upper Pliocene middle/upper Pleistocene continental deposits. The two basins are delimited near the northern margin of the Alpi Apuane by a SW-NE/WSW-ENE oriented transverse structure (called the Marciano-Minucciano strike-slip fault by Scandone, 2007), which according to Scandone (2007) acted as a dextral transfer accommodating the sinistral offset of the basin axes and of the marginal faults.
sections.OPEN QUESTIONS:
1) What are the structural relationships between the Sources in the Lunigiana basin?
2) What are the structural relationships between the Sources bordering the Lunigiana and Garfagnana basins?
sections.SUMMARIES:
Raggi (1985)
The author suggests a morphological evolution of Lunigiana basin and of the westernmost La Spezia gulf in the upper Pliocene -Pleistocene interval, on the basis of the analysis of the lacustrine and fluvio-lacustrine deposits and of their relationships with the substratum. Some evolutional phases are identified: a compressional Tortonian phase during which the NW-SE striking synclines and anticlines are formed. One of these anticlines borders the Lunigiana to the NE. During this phase, also some transversal (i.e. SW-NE striking) structures with strike-slip kinematic were formed. During the first stage, the rivers followed the trend of the compressional structures. Starting from the Villafranchian (upper Pliocene -lower Pleistocene) the area has been reached by extension (on the basis of the age of the lacustrine sediments) which generated the present shape of the graben.
The normal faults have the same strike as the axis of the compressional structures, those which border the SW margin of the graben are less inclined then those bordering the NE margin, generating an asymmetric graben with the master fault dipping towards NE. According to the author the maximum offset reach 2000 m and it decreases from SE towards NW.
Bernini (1991)
The extensional structures of Lunigiana are described as NW-SE striking normal faults with strikes similar to those of the compressional structures.
The master faults of the Val di Magra and La Spezia are described as listric normal faults dipping towards NE. The author suggest that the normal faults negatively reactivated the pre-existing thrust faults and that the SW-NE striking strike-slip faults play a role of trasfer faults between the normal fault segments. This interpretation is also in accordance with some SE-NW striking faults with transtensional kinematics at the outcrop scale.
According to the author's interpretation, the Val di Magra graben evolves towards the SE into the Garfagnana and the La Spezia grabens.
Boncio et al. (2000)
They use surface and subsurface geological data, as well as an analysis of the instrumental seismicity to describe the geometry and the possible seismogenic characteristics of the Alto Tiberina Fault (ATF). The ATF is a low-angle, NE-dipping normal fault that can be mapped for a length of more than 70 km, and belongs to the regional NE-dipping Etrurian normal fault system (EFS).
The EFS runs from northern Tuscany to southern Umbria, and its individual fault segment are associated with the main extensional basins of the northern Apennines.
The authors suggest that the EFS controls active extension and seismic release all along this stretch of the Apennines.
Bernini and Papani (2002)
These Authors have recognized along the western margin of the Lunigiana basin a number of Adriatic-dipping low-angle faults (Coloretta, Monteroggio and Mulazzo fault systems) and along the eastern margin several Tyrrhenian-dipping high-angle faults (Mocrone, Argenzio and Groppodalosio fault systems). Maximum down-throws have been observed across the Mulazzo fault system (more than 2500 meters of vertical displacement) and across the Groppodalosio fault system (about 2000 m of vertical displacement in the Compione area, with decreasing values moving towards the NW).
Scandone (2007)
In the framework of the 2005-2007 INGV-DPC S2 project, the research unit led by Scandone performed a seismotectonic investigation in Garfagnana and Lunigiana basins, based on stratigraphic and structural field analyses and on the interpretation of a set of commercial lines which includes dip and strike reflection profiles. The seismic profiles have been tied to two exploratory wells, the Pontremoli 1 well and the Lama dei Cerri 1 well. The results of this study allowed to identify faults displaying evidence of recent activity. Both in Lunigiana and Garfagnana the faults classified as faults with recent activity include an Adriatic-dipping low-angle fault which acts as a master fault, and a number of Tyrrhenian-dipping high-angle faults playing the role of antithetic faults. The two faults meet at a depth of about 1 sec TWT. In Lunigiana, the Adriatic-dipping master fault coincides with the Mulazzo system of Bernini and Papani (2002).
